title: Netanyahu’s Party Fuels Unverified “Stolen Election” Claims Against Arab-Led Parties in Israel
body:
Jerusalem – Israel’s political landscape remains in limbo after the nation’s fifth election in two years failed to deliver a clear governing majority. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party emerged as the largest bloc but fell short of the 61 seats needed to command a Knesset, while his chief challenger, former Defense Minister Gadi Eisenkot, led a centrist alliance that also missed the mark. The inconclusive results have sparked a heated debate over the role of Arab‑led parties, with Netanyahu’s camp repeatedly asserting, without evidence, that these parties have “stolen” the election by siphoning votes that would otherwise have bolstered the right‑wing bloc.

The final tally, released early Friday, gave Likud 32 seats, a modest gain from the previous vote but still well below the threshold for a stable coalition. Eisenkot’s National Unity list secured 24 seats, while the centrist Yesh Atid party, led by Yair Lapid, captured 19. Arab parties combined for 10 seats, a figure that, while historically consistent, has become a political flashpoint. Netanyahu’s spokesperson, Jonathan Nir, claimed the Arab parties “deliberately undermined the will of the Jewish majority,” a charge that political analysts say is more rhetorical than factual. The Arab parties, which include the United Arab List‑Ra’am and the Joint List, have consistently advocated for a Palestinian state and social reforms, positions that differ from the right‑wing agenda but do not equate to election fraud.

The accusations have inflamed an already volatile atmosphere. Netanyahu’s Likud, which has governed for most of the past decade, has leaned heavily on nationalist rhetoric and a hard‑line stance toward the Palestinian territories. By framing the Arab vote as a “theft,” the prime minister hopes to rally his base and pressure potential coalition partners to distance themselves from Arab parties. However, Israel’s fragmented party system and the legal requirement that any coalition must command a majority of Knesset members mean that excluding the Arab bloc could prove impossible. Historically, Arab parties have been tolerated as “outside” supporters in right‑leaning governments, but they have never been granted ministerial portfolios.

Eisenkot, whose centrist platform emphasizes security, economic revival, and a pragmatic approach to the Palestinian issue, has dismissed Netanyahu’s narrative as a distraction. In a televised interview, Eisenkot warned that “political point‑scoring” over the Arab vote threatens the country’s democratic fabric and could deepen societal divisions. He also signaled openness to negotiating a coalition that includes Arab parties, provided they commit to Israel’s security imperatives. Such a stance could make him a more attractive partner for parties like Yesh Atid and Labor, which have expressed willingness to work across ideological lines.

Political scientists note that the current impasse reflects deeper structural challenges within Israel’s parliamentary system. The low electoral threshold of 3.25 % encourages the proliferation of small parties, making it difficult for any single bloc to achieve a decisive majority. Moreover, the repeated election cycles have exhausted voters, leading to lower turnout and heightened polarization. The “stolen election” rhetoric may therefore be a tactical move to deflect criticism of Netanyahu’s inability to secure a coalition after multiple attempts.

As the clock ticks toward the constitutional deadline for forming a government, both Likud and National Unity are expected to engage in intensive behind‑the‑scenes negotiations with smaller parties, including the ultra‑Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism factions, as well as the centrist Yesh Atid. The Arab parties, while unlikely to receive ministerial posts, could still wield influence as kingmakers if either side needs their support to reach the 61‑seat threshold. Observers caution that any coalition formed under such strained circumstances will face significant hurdles in passing legislation, especially on contentious issues like judicial reforms and the ongoing conflict with the Palestinians.

The coming weeks will determine whether Israel can break the cycle of dead‑locked elections or descend further into political instability. If Netanyahu’s narrative fails to translate into tangible coalition offers, the likelihood of a new election looms, prolonging uncertainty for a nation already grappling with security challenges and deep societal divides. Conversely, a pragmatic alliance that incorporates Arab parties, even in a limited capacity, could signal a shift toward a more inclusive, albeit fragile, governing arrangement. The outcome will shape not only Israel’s domestic policy agenda but also its diplomatic posture in a volatile Middle‑East region.
